title: The rains begin
hook: Asalha Puja marks the first sermon; the rains retreat starts the next day

segments.voice: Yesterday: Poson, Mahinda and the mango tree. Your line: who brought it.

In India, the monsoon doesn't drizzle. It arrives. Roads turn to rivers, fields to mud, and anything walking on the ground, worms, insects, frogs, comes up into the open. In the Buddha's time, wandering teachers of many kinds stopped traveling for these months. Buddhist monks, early on, kept walking. People complained, the Vinaya says: these monks trample the green shoots and crush small creatures. So the Buddha set a rule: stay in one place for the rains. And the full moon just before the rains carries its own memory, the very first teaching.

In the Theravada tradition, the full moon of the month Asalha, usually in July, is the anniversary of the first sermon. Two months after his awakening, tradition says, the Buddha found his five former companions in the Deer Park near Benares and set the wheel of the teaching in motion: the middle way, the four noble truths. One of the five, Kondanna, understood, the first of them to see it. With that, the tradition says, the three jewels were complete: the Buddha, the teaching and the community. Thailand, Laos and Cambodia mark the day as Asalha Puja; in Thailand it's a national holiday. People go to the temple, hear the first sermon chanted, and walk three times around the shrine holding candles. The very next day the rains retreat begins: Vassa, a word that means rain, and also year, because a monk's seniority was counted in rains. For three lunar months, monks stay in one monastery. Some lay people take up something for the season too: giving up alcohol, keeping more precepts, meditating daily, coming to the temple on every moon day. In Thailand it's a custom for young men to ordain for one Vassa, as a rite of passage. For a monastery, it's the quiet season of study and practice, with nowhere to go. There's a gentle wisdom in it: weather you can't change becomes a season you use.
screen: `THE FIRST SERMON'S FULL MOON.` · `KONDANNA UNDERSTANDS.` · `VASSA: THREE MONTHS IN ONE PLACE.` · then, large: `THE RAINS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself what you could keep for one season, something small enough to last: five minutes of sitting each morning, no phone in bed, one kind message a week, fewer drinks. Let a few options come, and notice which one feels right rather than heroic. Then choose it, quietly, here.
vassa. The Pali word for rain, the rainy season, and a year: Asalha Puja remembers the first sermon on the full moon, and the next day the three-month rains retreat begins. Today's word.
Your line: choose this season's practice. Small is fine, as long as it lasts. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Asalha Puja, Buddhists in Thailand, Laos and Cambodia gather at temples to hear the first sermon and circle the shrine with candles; during the following three-month Vassa, monks stay in one monastery and some lay people take on extra practices.

chat.says: Why do Buddhist monks stay put for three months each year?
options: The Buddha set it so they'd stop trampling crops and creatures in the rains.
The Buddha set it as a penance for monks who had broken the rules.
It's when they walk to every village to teach before the floods.
